# Generative AI, in Its Simplest Form {.unnumbered}

*Standalone tutorial accompanying [W02](../weeks/w02.qmd). Interactive version:
[Sampling as a Map](../materials/sampling-as-a-map.html).*

This note presents the same tiny generator twice — first as a **hierarchy you sample
conditionally** (a Bayesian model), then as a **deterministic map applied to uniform
randomness** — and then makes the claim that carries the rest of the course: every modern
generative sampler, diffusion included, is the second picture — once all of its
random inputs are exposed — with a learned ingredient in place of the formula.

## View 1: conditional generation (a hierarchical model)

The simplest latent-variable model:

$$
\mathbb{P}(z = 1) = \pi, \quad \mathbb{P}(z = 2) = 1 - \pi, \qquad
x \mid z \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(\mu_z,\, \sigma^2).
$$

**Ancestral sampling** generates by following the arrows: draw the latent coin $z$,
then draw $x$ from the selected component. The observed marginal is obtained by
summing out the latent:

$$
p(x) \;=\; \sum_{z} p(z)\, p(x \mid z)
\;=\; \pi\, \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_1, \sigma^2) + (1-\pi)\, \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_2, \sigma^2)
$$

— exactly the two-component mixture from the playground. A mixture is not just a
formula; it is a *generative story*: population $\to$ subpopulation $\to$ individual.

**Inference is the same hierarchy, run backwards.** Given an observed $x$, Bayes'
rule gives the posterior over the hidden coin:

$$
\mathbb{P}(z = 1 \mid x)
= \frac{\pi\, \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_1, \sigma^2)}
       {\pi\, \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_1, \sigma^2) + (1-\pi)\, \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_2, \sigma^2)} .
$$

For $\mu_{1,2} = \mp 1$ and $\pi = \tfrac12$ this equals
$\operatorname{sigmoid}(-2x/\sigma^2)$; its companion
$\mathbb{P}(z = 2 \mid x) = \operatorname{sigmoid}(2x/\sigma^2)$ is exactly the
posterior W01 computed for the $+1$ component, and the posterior mean of $\mu_z$ is
the tanh denoiser: **W01's denoising step was latent-variable inference all along.**
Generation and inference are the two directions of one arrow.

## View 2: the coin disappears into a map

**Theorem (inverse-CDF / probability integral transform).** Let $F$ be a CDF with
generalized inverse $F^{-1}(u) = \inf\{x : F(x) \ge u\}$, and let
$U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$. Then $X = F^{-1}(U)$ has CDF $F$.

*Proof.* $\mathbb{P}(F^{-1}(U) \le x) = \mathbb{P}(U \le F(x)) = F(x)$, since
$F^{-1}(u) \le x \iff u \le F(x)$ by monotonicity. $\square$

For our mixture, $F(x) = \pi\,\Phi\!\big(\tfrac{x-\mu_1}{\sigma}\big) +
(1-\pi)\,\Phi\!\big(\tfrac{x-\mu_2}{\sigma}\big)$ is continuous and strictly
increasing, so $F^{-1}$ is an honest function, and

$$
u \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1), \qquad x = F^{-1}(u)
$$

generates the mixture **with no coin anywhere** — the explicit coin has been
marginalized out. One caution about where it went: under this map, the event
$u < \pi$ selects the lowest $\pi$-fraction of the *mixture* distribution, which is
**not** the same as the ancestral label $z = 1$ when the components overlap — both
Gaussians have full support, so each contributes on both sides of any quantile. (In
the well-separated limit $\sigma \to 0$ the two events do coincide, and the *packed*
map below is the construction in which $u < \pi$ genuinely encodes the coin.)
Randomness in, structure out, everything in between deterministic.

## The two-point limit

Send $\sigma \to 0$ with $\mu_{1,2} = \mp 1$. The CDF collapses to a staircase: a jump
of height $\pi$ at $-1$, a flat **plateau** at height $\pi$ across the empty middle, a
jump to $1$ at $+1$. The map becomes

$$
x = \begin{cases} -1, & u < \pi \\ +1, & u > \pi \end{cases}
\qquad\text{i.e.}\quad x = \operatorname{sign}(u - \pi),
$$

W01's dataset, generated by thresholding a uniform (almost surely: the single point
$u = \pi$ has probability zero). The plateau is the geometric image of the empty
region: no value of $u$ lands there. [The Deterministic Map, Proved](./map-proved.qmd) proves this limit. (In the demo, slide $\sigma$ down
and watch the staircase form.)

## Maps are not unique

$F^{-1}$ is the *monotone* map pushing $\text{Uniform}(0,1)$ to $p$, but not the only
map. The "packed" two-stage construction

$$
x = \begin{cases}
\mu_1 + \sigma\, \Phi^{-1}\!\big(u/\pi\big), & u < \pi,\\[2pt]
\mu_2 + \sigma\, \Phi^{-1}\!\big(\tfrac{u-\pi}{1-\pi}\big), & u \ge \pi,
\end{cases}
$$

also pushes uniform to the mixture (each branch rescales its segment of $[0,1]$ back
to a full uniform — Exercise 3), and it is *literally* ancestral sampling written as
one formula. Different map, same distribution: what is canonical is the
*distribution*, not the transport. (In higher dimensions, choosing among the many
maps is its own subject — optimal transport — which we will brush against later.)

## The claim that organizes everything

> **Once all of its random draws are exposed, a generative sampler is a
> deterministic map from base randomness to a sample.**

| Model | Random input(s) | Sampling mechanism | Typical fitting |
|---|---|---|---|
| This note | $u \sim \text{U}(0,1)$ | quantile $F^{-1}(u)$ (numerical in the demo) | the CDF is known |
| GAN | $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ | $G_\theta(z)$, a network | adversarial objective |
| VAE | $z$, plus decoder noise $\varepsilon$ | sample $p_\theta(x \mid z)$, i.e. $T_\theta(z, \varepsilon)$ | ELBO / variational learning |
| Normalizing flow | $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ | invertible $f_\theta(z)$ | exact likelihood (change of variables) |
| **Diffusion** | $x_T \sim \mathcal{N}$; step noise if stochastic | **probability-flow ODE** (deterministic) or reverse SDE | **score/denoising objectives, ELBO** |

: {tbl-colwidths="[18,24,32,26]"}

The outer skeleton is shared — simple randomness, a sampling mechanism, data — while
the learned object, the structural constraints, and the sampler differ. For diffusion
in particular, determinism is a *sampler choice*: the probability-flow ODE is a
deterministic map from $x_T$; the reverse SDE consumes fresh noise at every step and
is a deterministic function only of $(x_T, \text{all step noises})$.

In one dimension with a known CDF, the map is a formula. For images, the population
law is unknown and no tractable multivariate inverse-CDF construction exists — so deep
generative models learn a *transport, density, score, or other ingredient* of a
sampler rather than writing the map down. And you have already run one: W01's
probability-flow ODE numerically transported a moment-matched Gaussian to within
$\approx \sigma_{\min}$ of the two-point data (W01 lists the approximations
involved); with the exact terminal law, score, and integration, it is an exact
deterministic transport — an inverse-CDF-like map built not from the CDF but from the
**score**, which is exactly the object a neural network can learn in high dimension.
That construction, done properly, is Modules 4–6.

## Exercises

1. Complete the inverse-CDF proof for a general (possibly non-strictly-increasing)
   $F$ using the generalized inverse.
2. Derive $\mathbb{P}(z = 1 \mid x)$ above, and show that for
   $\mu_{1,2} = \mp 1$, $\sigma = 1$, $\pi = \tfrac12$ its companion
   $\mathbb{P}(z = 2 \mid x)$ equals W01's $\operatorname{sigmoid}(2x)$ posterior
   (mind which component carries the $+$ sign); compute the posterior mean of
   $\mu_z$.
3. Verify the packed map: show that conditional on $u < \pi$, the rescaled variable
   $u/\pi$ is $\text{Uniform}(0,1)$, and conclude that the branch produces
   $\mathcal{N}(\mu_1, \sigma^2)$ with the correct probability.
4. Construct the inverse-CDF map for a **three**-component mixture and describe its
   staircase limit as $\sigma \to 0$. How many plateaus, at what heights?
5. The map $x = F^{-1}(u)$ is monotone increasing. Exhibit a *decreasing* map with
   the same pushforward, and a map that is neither monotone nor continuous. (Hint:
   $1 - u$ is also uniform.)
